owner.occupation: Pack-house supervisor at an export rose farm

world.bio: I supervise the pack-house at an export rose farm on Lake Naivasha. We ship to Amsterdam every week. I run the grading lines: stems are sorted by length, bud size and quality, bunched and boxed for the Dutch auction. I know the residue paperwork for every bed by heart. I'm saving for my daughter's boarding school fees and sing in my church choir on Sundays.
skills_assets: Supervise a pack-house of 140 workers across three grading lines
Knowledge of EU residue and phytosanitary compliance records
Experience with cold chain and flower grading standards
Contacts in the farm's quality and agronomy teams
A good reputation with the Dutch buyers' agents

projects.name: Reject stem disposal
projects.text: Every week about two tonnes of export-rejected stems (short, bent, bruised petals) go into the compost pit; the Dutch buyer won't take them. The compost pit is filling up and smelling. Management wants a solution but doesn't know what.

projects.name: Daughter's school fees
projects.text: Grace is 14 and at a boarding school in Nakuru. Fees are KES 95,000 a term. I'm saving each month, short by about 20,000 this term.

projects.name: Commute disruption
projects.text: A road washout between Naivasha town and the farm doubled my matatu commute. Leaving at 4:30 am now.

notes.text: Grading line two ran slow today. Too many short stems. Valentine's orders are coming in October for the early shipment, so we need volume. Workers are tired.
Walked past the compost pit at the end of shift. The smell was sharp. About two tonnes of rejects this week, same as last. Management says the pit is nearly full and we need a plan.
Church choir rehearsal. We're learning a new hymn in Kikuyu. My alto line is tricky. I got it right once and the choir leader smiled.
The matatu was late again. Mud on the road, driver detoured through the village. I arrived 40 minutes late and my line was already running.
Spoke to the agronomist about the residue records. He said every bed has spray records, including the reject stems, for EU compliance. I had to remind him that the buyer sometimes asks for them.
Grace called from school. She needs a new uniform and a calculator. I said I'd send money by Friday. After sending it I had 800 shillings left.
The Dutch agent sent a message: rejection rate this month is 12%. Last month it was 9%. I need to look at line three.
Lunch break conversation: one of the workers said her cousin dries the rejected petals and sells them at the market as potpourri. I laughed, then thought maybe it's not a bad idea.
Tried to count how many stems go in the pit each week: roughly 25,000. If even a third could be used, it would be something.
Rain again. The farm road has potholes. The truck carrying boxes to the airport was late; we stayed until 9 pm.

messages.text: Manager: Wanjiru, what's the plan for the reject pile? Me: I don't have one. Manager: We need something before the rainy season. Me: I'll think.
Peter: The residue records for all beds are up to date, including rejects. Me: Good. Peter: Buyers sometimes ask. Me: I know.
Grace: Mum, can you send money for my calculator? Me: How much? Grace: 1,500. Me: I'll send it today.
Leader: We need altos on Sunday. Me: I'll be there. Leader: Bring your sister. Me: She's busy.
Joyce: Line three has too many bruised petals. Me: Check the cold room temperature. Joyce: It's 3°C. Me: Let me look.

constraints: Time: pack-house shift 5am-3pm, longer in peak season
Cannot speak for farm management on commercial decisions
sensitive: Worried about job security if rejection rates keep rising

disclosure_policy.t0_public: Pack-house supervisor at an export rose farm; about two tonnes of export-rejected stems go into the compost pit every week; the Dutch buyer won't take them
disclosure_policy.t2_after_trust: Spray and residue records for every bed, including rejects
